column1: # Confusable words (헷갈리는 어휘): groups of two to four near-synonyms or look-alikes that advanced learners (TOPIK 5-6) mix up:
# spelling confusables, near-synonyms and a few grammar look-alikes. Shown in the app under Lists > Study lists > Writing & usage.
# AI-written (Claude): every field below is AI-drafted. Rows ship only after an independent review (content-review skill; the
# checklist is pipeline/qa/writing_confusables_review.md) marks them `approved...` in the review column; the app labels them AI.
# Tab-separated, one group per row (file order = order in the app).
#   id            C001...: stable id for the reviewer's notes
#   kind          spelling (sound-alike or look-alike spellings) | meaning (near-synonyms) | grammar (endings, particles, spacing)
#   words         the two to four words, separated by " | ". A leading × means a WRONG spelling that
#                 people write, shown struck through; it has no sentence. A group needs at least one correct word.
#   explanation_en  how the words differ (English; Korean words in quotes)
#   ex_ko         one model sentence per word, separated by " | ", in the order of `words` ("-" for a wrong spelling)
#   ex_en         the English of each sentence, same order and separators ("-" for a wrong spelling)
#   mistake_en    the common mistake in one line (English; Korean in quotes)
#   review        draft | approved[: who/date] | rejected: reason. Only `approved...` rows ship.
# Dictionary links are not stored: the build looks each correct word up as a headword (krdict first) and keeps the entry it finds.

column4: explanation_en
column5: ex_ko
column6: ex_en
column7: mistake_en

column4: “반드시” is an adverb meaning “without fail, certainly”. “반듯이” comes from “반듯하다” and means “straight, neatly, upright”. They sound almost alike but have nothing in common in meaning.
column5: 약속은 반드시 지켜야 한다. | 허리를 반듯이 펴고 앉았다.
column6: A promise must be kept without fail. | He sat with his back held straight.
column7: Writing “반듯이” for “certainly”. If you can replace it with “꼭 / 틀림없이”, use “반드시”.

column4: “결재” (決裁) is approval of a plan or document by a person with authority. “결제” (決濟) is settling a payment or an account. In everyday life they are mixed up most with card payments.
column5: 부장님께 보고서를 올려 결재를 받았다. | 카드로 대금을 결제했다.
column6: I got the report approved by my department head. | I paid the bill by card.
column7: Writing “카드 결재” for a card payment; it is always “카드 결제”.

column4: “개발” (開發) is to develop something new or to open up land, resources and technology. “계발” (啓發) is to develop what is already inside a person: talent, potential, intelligence.
column5: 회사는 새로운 소프트웨어를 개발했다. | 학생들의 창의력을 계발하는 교육이 필요하다.
column6: The company developed new software. | Education that develops students' creativity is needed.
column7: Using “개발” for talents and “계발” for products. “자기 계발” (self-improvement) is the set phrase; many people also write “자기 개발”, which dictionaries now accept too, but in a test stay with “계발” for abilities.

column4: “지양” (止揚) means to avoid or stop doing something (the thing you give up). “지향” (志向) means to aim at something (the direction you head in). They are near opposites but sound alike.
column5: 일회용품 사용은 지양해야 한다. | 우리 학교는 학생 중심의 교육을 지향한다.
column6: The use of disposable items should be avoided. | Our school aims for student-centred education.
column7: Writing “과소비를 지향하다” to mean avoid overspending. The thing you avoid goes with “지양”, the goal with “지향”.

column4: “혼동” is to mix up two things and take one for the other. “혼돈” is chaos, a state with no order (often of the world or society). “혼란” is confusion or disorder that people feel or cause.
column5: 두 단어의 뜻을 혼동하기 쉽다. | 전쟁 직후 사회는 혼돈 상태에 빠졌다. | 갑작스러운 발표로 시장에 혼란이 일어났다.
column6: It is easy to confuse the meanings of the two words. | Right after the war, society fell into chaos. | The sudden announcement caused confusion in the market.
column7: Writing “혼돈하다” for “to confuse (one thing for another)”; the verb is “혼동하다”. “혼돈” is a noun for chaos.

column4: Both are written 一切. “일체” means “everything, all”. “일절” means “not at all, entirely” and is used only with a negative or a ban.
column5: 이 행사에 드는 비용 일체는 회사가 부담한다. | 이곳에서는 흡연을 일절 금지한다.
column6: The company bears all the costs of this event. | Smoking is strictly forbidden here.
column7: Using “일체” with a negative (“일체 안 된다”). With a negative or a ban, say “일절”.

column4: “체제” (體制) is the structure of a country or an organisation: “정치 체제”, “경제 체제”. “체계” (體系) is a set of things arranged in a logical order: “교육 체계”, “체계적으로”. “체재” (滯在) is staying in a place away from home for a while.
column5: 그 나라는 민주주의 체제를 유지하고 있다. | 학습한 내용을 체계 있게 정리해야 한다. | 그는 출장으로 한 달간 파리에 체재했다.
column6: That country maintains a democratic system of government. | You have to organise what you learn in a systematic way. | He stayed in Paris for a month on a business trip.
column7: Writing “체제적으로” for “systematically”; the adverb is “체계적으로”.

column4: “실재” (實在) is real existence, being there in fact: “실재하다”. “실제” (實際) means the real situation or what actually happens, as against theory or rumour: “실제로”, “실제 상황”.
column5: 신화에 나오는 동물은 실재하지 않는다. | 실제로 가 보니 소문과 달랐다.
column6: The animals in myths do not exist. | When I actually went there, it was different from the rumours.
column7: Writing “실재로” for “in fact”; the adverb is “실제로”. “실재” is the verb root “실재하다” (to exist).

column4: “재고” (再考) is to think again and reconsider. “제고” (提高) is to raise a level, quality or awareness.
column5: 이 계획은 재고할 필요가 있다. | 서비스의 질을 제고하기 위해 노력해야 한다.
column6: This plan needs to be reconsidered. | We must make efforts to raise the quality of service.
column7: Writing “재고” for “raise” (“질을 재고하다”). Raising something is “제고”. Another “재고” (在庫, stock in the warehouse) is a third word.

column4: Both come from 更新. “갱신” means renewing or updating something so that it continues: “계약 갱신”, “여권 갱신”. “경신” means breaking a record by setting a new one: “기록 경신”.
column5: 이번 달에 운전면허를 갱신해야 한다. | 선수가 세계 기록을 경신했다.
column6: I have to renew my driving licence this month. | The athlete broke the world record.
column7: Writing “기록 갱신” for breaking a record (common in news); strictly it is “기록 경신”.

column4: “부문” is a category or field into which something is divided: “연기 부문”, “경제 부문”. “부분” is a part of a whole: “앞부분”, “일부분”.
column5: 그는 연기 부문에서 상을 받았다. | 이 글의 앞부분은 이해하기 쉽다.
column6: He won an award in the acting category. | The first part of this text is easy to understand.
column7: Writing “부분별 수상자” for the winners by category; the divisions of a field are “부문”.

column4: “한참” is a fairly long time or distance (“한참 동안”). “한창” is the height of something, its peak (“한창 -고 있다”, “한창때”).
column5: 그는 한참 동안 아무 말도 하지 않았다. | 지금은 벚꽃이 한창이다.
column6: He did not say a word for quite a while. | The cherry blossoms are now in full bloom.
column7: Writing “한창 동안” for “for a long time”. A span of time is “한참 동안”.

column4: The noun from “바라다” (to wish) is “바람”. “바램” is a very common wrong form. The verb stem is “바라-”, so “바라요”, not “×바래요”.
column5: 나의 가장 큰 바람은 가족의 건강이다. | -
column6: My greatest wish is my family's health. | -
column7: Writing “바램” for “wish” and “바래요” for “I hope”. Correct: “바람”, “바라요”.

column4: “금세” is short for “금시에” and means “soon, in no time”. “금새” is a different, rare word meaning the price of an item.
column5: 아이는 눕자마자 금세 잠이 들었다. | 시장마다 채소의 금새가 조금씩 다르다.
column6: The child fell asleep in no time after lying down. | The price of vegetables differs a little from market to market.
column7: Writing “금새” for “soon”. “금방” and “금세” both mean “right away”; “금새” is not one of them.

column4: There is no word “몇 일”. “며칠” is the one word used both for “how many days” and “what date”.
column5: 며칠 동안 비가 계속 내렸다. | -
column6: It kept raining for several days. | -
column7: Writing “몇 일” (“오늘이 몇 일이에요?”). Always “며칠”.

column4: “오랜만” means “after a long time” (a shortened form of “오래간만”) and goes with “에”. “오랫동안” means “for a long time” and is written as one word with a “ㅅ” in the middle.
column5: 오랜만에 고향 친구를 만났다. | 그는 오랫동안 한국에서 살았다.
column6: I met a hometown friend after a long time. | He has lived in Korea for a long time.
column7: Writing “×오랫만에” (with “ㅅ”). The correct form is “오랜만에”.

column4: The verb is “설레다” (to flutter with excitement); the noun is “설렘”. Writing “설레이다” or “설레임” is a common mistake.
column5: 첫 출근을 앞두고 가슴이 설렌다. | -
column6: My heart flutters on the eve of my first day at work. | -
column7: Writing “가슴이 설레인다” or “설레임”. Correct: “설렌다”, “설렘”.

column4: The verb is “헤매다” (to wander about, to be lost). Its stem is “헤매-”: “헤맨다”, “헤맸다”.
column5: 길을 몰라 한참을 헤맸다. | -
column6: I didn't know the way and wandered around for a long time. | -
column7: Writing “헤메다 / 헤멨다”. Correct: “헤매다 / 헤맸다”.

column4: “삼가다” is a verb in itself (to refrain, to be careful). Do not add “-하다”. The adverb “삼가” (respectfully) is a different word.
column5: 공공장소에서는 큰 소리로 말하는 것을 삼가시기 바랍니다. | -
column6: Please refrain from talking loudly in public places. | -
column7: Writing “삼가하다 / 삼가해 주십시오”. Correct: “삼가다 / 삼가 주십시오”.

column4: “무릅쓰다” means to endure something difficult or dangerous and go on. It has nothing to do with “무릎” (the knee).
column5: 그는 위험을 무릅쓰고 아이를 구했다. | -
column6: He risked danger to save the child. | -
column7: Writing “무릎쓰고”. Correct: “무릅쓰고”.

column4: Adverb endings follow a rule. After a stem with a “ㅅ” final consonant (“깨끗하다”) or a reduplicated noun (“틈틈”, “곳곳”, “집집”) the ending is “-이”. After other stems that end in “-하다” (“꼼꼼하다”, “조용하다”) it is “-히”.
column5: 손을 깨끗이 씻었다. | 계약서를 꼼꼼히 읽어 보았다. | 틈틈이 책을 읽는 습관이 필요하다.
column6: I washed my hands clean. | I read the contract carefully. | You need the habit of reading in your spare moments.
column7: Writing “깨끗히” or “꼼꼼이”. Rule of thumb: “ㅅ” final or repeated noun → “-이”; other “-하다” words → “-히”.

column4: After a vowel or “ㄴ”, the suffix 率 is written “율” (“비율”, “이자율”, “백분율”). After any other consonant, it is “률” (“확률”, “성공률”, “출석률”).
column5: 전체에서 여성이 차지하는 비율이 높다. | 내일 비가 올 확률은 30%이다.
column6: The proportion of women in the total is high. | The probability of rain tomorrow is 30%.
column7: Writing “비률 / 확율”. The “률/율” rule depends on the sound before it (vowel or “ㄴ → 율”).

column4: “어떻게” is the adverb “how”. “어떡해” is a contraction of “어떻게 해” and stands on its own as “what should I do?”.
column5: 이 문제를 어떻게 풀어야 할까? | 지갑을 잃어버렸는데 어떡해!
column6: How should I solve this problem? | I lost my wallet, what do I do!
column7: Writing “어떻게!” as an exclamation of distress or “어떡게”. Distress is “어떡해”.

column4: “웬” (from “어찌 된”) modifies a noun: “웬일”, “웬 사람”. “왠지” is a contraction of “왜인지” and means “for some reason”. “왠” only appears in “왠지”.
column5: 이게 웬 일이니? | 오늘은 왠지 기분이 좋다.
column6: What on earth is this? | For some reason I feel good today.
column7: Writing “왠일” (correct: “웬일”) or “웬지” (correct: “왠지”).

column4: “안” is a short form of “아니” and comes before a verb or adjective: “안 가다”. “않다” is a verb that follows “-지”: “가지 않다”. Both give the same negation.
column5: 나는 커피를 안 마신다. | 나는 커피를 마시지 않는다.
column6: I don't drink coffee. | I don't drink coffee.
column7: Writing “않 먹었다” or “먹지 안 았다”. “않-” only appears in “-지 않다”; the short “안” goes before the verb.

column4: “돼” is the contraction of “되어”. A quick test: replace with “하 / 해”. If “하” fits, write “되”; if “해” fits, write “돼”.
column5: 그는 꿈을 이루어 의사가 되었다. | 이제 그만 가도 돼.
column6: He fulfilled his dream and became a doctor. | You can leave now.
column7: Writing “안 되요 / 되서 / 되요”. Correct: “안 돼요 / 돼서 / 돼요”.

column4: “안되다” (one word) is an adjective: to feel sorry for, or to go badly (“일이 안되다”, “안됐다”). “안 되다” (spaced) is the negation of “되다”: not become, not be allowed.
column5: 그 소식을 들으니 참 안됐다. | 이곳에서는 사진을 찍으면 안 된다.
column6: I felt very sorry to hear that news. | You must not take photos here.
column7: Writing “사진을 찍으면 안되요”. “Not allowed” is “안 돼요” (two words).

column4: “못하다” (one word) means “to be bad at” (“노래를 못하다”) or “cannot at all”. “못 하다” (spaced) means that someone cannot do it because of circumstances.
column5: 그는 노래를 못해서 노래방에 가지 않는다. | 몸이 아파서 숙제를 못 했다.
column6: He is bad at singing, so he does not go to karaoke. | I could not do my homework because I was sick.
column7: Mixing the two spellings. Rule of thumb: skill or level → “못하다”; cannot because of circumstances → “못 하다”.

column4: “-(으)ㄴ 지” (spaced; “지” is a noun for time) means “since …”: “온 지 3년”. “-(으)ㄴ지” (attached) is an ending for an indirect question or doubt: “맞는지 모르다”.
column5: 한국에 온 지 3년이 되었다. | 이것이 맞는지 확인해 보았다.
column6: It has been three years since I came to Korea. | I checked whether this is right.
column7: Writing “온지 3년이 되었다” or “맞는 지 확인했다”. “Since” needs a space; “whether” does not.

column4: “받치다” is to hold up from below (“우산을 받치다”). “받히다” is the passive of “받다”: to be butted or hit. “바치다” is to offer or devote (“목숨을 바치다”).
column5: 책 밑에 받침을 받쳐 놓았다. | 그는 소에게 받혀 크게 다쳤다. | 그는 평생을 연구에 바쳤다.
column6: I propped a stand underneath the book. | He was gored by a bull and badly hurt. | He devoted his whole life to research.
column7: Writing “소에게 받쳤다” (should be “받혔다”) or “목숨을 받쳤다” (should be “바쳤다”).

column4: “부딪치다” is active: to strike something, or two things strike each other. “부딪히다” is passive: to be struck, or to run into something such as an obstacle (“차에 부딪히다”, “난관에 부딪히다”).
column5: 두 사람이 모퉁이에서 서로 부딪쳤다. | 사업은 시작부터 큰 어려움에 부딪혔다.
column6: The two people bumped into each other at the corner. | The business ran into great difficulties from the start.
column7: Writing “어려움에 부딪쳤다” where you mean you ran into difficulty. The thing that stops you hits you: “부딪히다”.

column4: “걷잡다” is to stop or hold back something that is spreading; it appears in “걷잡을 수 없다” (cannot be stopped). “겉잡다” is to estimate roughly (“겉잡아 말하다”).
column5: 불길이 걷잡을 수 없이 번졌다. | 이 일은 겉잡아도 사흘은 걸린다.
column6: The fire spread out of control. | This job will take at least three days, even at a rough estimate.
column7: Writing “겉잡을 수 없다”; it is always “걷잡을 수 없다”.

column4: “띄다” is to catch the eye (“눈에 띄다”) or to leave a gap (“간격을 띄다”). “띠다” is to wear or carry something with you: “미소를 띠다”, “붉은빛을 띠다”, “임무를 띠다”.
column5: 거리에서 눈에 띄는 간판을 발견했다. | 그의 얼굴은 미소를 띠고 있었다.
column6: I spotted a conspicuous sign on the street. | His face wore a smile.
column7: Writing “미소를 띄다” or “눈에 띠다”. The verb that carries a colour or an expression is “띠다”.

column4: “쫓다” is to chase after or drive away (“도둑을 쫓다”, “파리를 쫓다”). “좇다” is to follow or pursue something abstract such as a dream, an ideal, or someone's advice.
column5: 경찰이 도망가는 도둑을 쫓았다. | 그는 오로지 돈만을 좇아 살아왔다.
column6: The police chased the fleeing thief. | He has lived pursuing nothing but money.
column7: Writing “꿈을 쫓다”. For goals, ideals and opinions, standard Korean prefers “좇다”, but “쫓다” is widely used.

column4: “바라다” is to hope for something that depends on events or on other people; it often takes “-기를 바라다”. “원하다” is to want something and ask for it; its object is a thing, a person or a state you could actually get.
column5: 나는 모든 사람이 행복하기를 바란다. | 그는 안정적인 직업을 원한다.
column6: I hope that everyone will be happy. | He wants a stable job.
column7: Writing “바래요 / 바램” (the stem is “바라-”: “바라요”, “바람”) and “-기를 원하다” for a hope that depends on others, where “-기를 바라다” is more natural.

column4: “다르다” means “different”: A is not the same as B. “틀리다” means “wrong, incorrect”, or something going wrong. They are one of the most common mix-ups in speech.
column5: 두 사람의 생각은 서로 다르다. | 이 문제의 답은 틀렸다.
column6: The two people's ideas differ from each other. | The answer to this question is wrong.
column7: Saying “생각이 틀리다” for “my opinion is different”. Use “틀리다” only for right/wrong.

column4: “맞추다” is to fit or adjust things to one another: “시간에 맞추다”, “입을 맞추다”, “답을 맞춰 보다” (compare answers). “맞히다” is to get something right or to hit a target: “정답을 맞히다”.
column5: 우리는 약속 시간에 맞추어 도착했다. | 그는 퀴즈의 정답을 모두 맞혔다.
column6: We arrived to fit in with the appointed time. | He got all the answers in the quiz right.
column7: Writing “정답을 맞췄다” for getting the correct answer; it is “맞혔다”. “답을 맞춰 보다” (check answers against each other) is correct.

column4: “가르치다” is to teach (someone a subject). “가리키다” is to point at something with a finger or an arrow. There is no word “가르키다”.
column5: 선생님은 학생들에게 한국어를 가르친다. | 그는 손가락으로 지도의 한 지점을 가리켰다.
column6: The teacher teaches Korean to the students. | He pointed to a spot on the map with his finger.
column7: Writing “가르키다” or “손가락으로 가르치다”. Pointing is “가리키다”.

column4: “늘이다” is to make longer by stretching: “고무줄을 늘이다”. “늘리다” is to increase quantity or size: “수를 늘리다”, “재산을 늘리다”.
column5: 그는 고무줄을 길게 늘여 보았다. | 정부는 일자리를 늘리겠다고 약속했다.
column6: He stretched the elastic band out long. | The government promised to increase the number of jobs.
column7: Writing “바지 길이를 늘렸다” (should be “늘였다”) or “인원을 늘였다” (should be “늘렸다”).

column4: “부치다” is to send (mail, money, a parcel) and also to fry (“전을 부치다”). “붙이다” is to stick on or attach, and also to add or start (“불을 붙이다”, “이름을 붙이다”).
column5: 어머니께 소포를 부쳤다. | 벽에 포스터를 붙였다.
column6: I sent a parcel to my mother. | I stuck a poster on the wall.
column7: Writing “편지를 붙였다” or “우표를 부쳤다”; it is “편지를 부쳤다” and “우표를 붙였다”.

column4: “이따가” is an adverb meaning “later, in a while”. “있다가” is “있다” + “-다가”: stay for a while and then do something else.
column5: 이따가 다시 연락드리겠습니다. | 집에 있다가 친구의 전화를 받고 나갔다.
column6: I will contact you again later. | I was at home when I got a call from a friend and went out.
column7: Writing “있다가 연락할게” for “later”. If you can say “나중에”, it is “이따가”; if “있다 + 가다 / 오다 …” follows, it is “있다가”.

column4: “그러므로” is a conjunction meaning “therefore” (“그러하다 + -므로”). “그럼으로(써)” means “by doing so”, “by that means”; it is “그렇게 하다 + -(으)ㅁ으로써”.
column5: 시간은 한정되어 있다. 그러므로 계획이 필요하다. | 그는 매일 연습했다. 그럼으로써 실력을 크게 높였다.
column6: Time is limited. Therefore a plan is necessary. | He practised every day, and by doing so he raised his skill greatly.
column7: Writing “그럼으로 인해 …” for “therefore”. Use “그러므로 / 따라서” for results and “그럼으로써” for “by doing that”.

column4: “-(ㄴ/는)대” is the contraction of “-다고 해”: I report what someone said. “-데” is the contraction of “-더라”: I report what I saw or heard myself. Both are spoken endings.
column5: 친구가 내일 비가 온대. | 어제 가 보니까 그 집 음식이 맛있데.
column6: My friend says it will rain tomorrow. | When I went there yesterday, their food was good.
column7: Using “-데” for something you were told. Hearsay is “-대”; what you witnessed is “-데”. Neither is for an essay.

column4: “계기” is the trigger or turning point that sets something in motion. “기회” is a chance or an opportunity that you can take.
column5: 그 책이 그가 작가가 되는 계기가 되었다. | 이번 방학은 외국어를 배울 좋은 기회이다.
column6: That book became the trigger for his becoming a writer. | These holidays are a good chance to learn a foreign language.
column7: Writing “계기를 얻다” for “get a chance”. A chance is “기회를 얻다”; a “계기” is what makes something happen.

column4: “경험” is the experience you accumulate through doing or living, including past knowledge. “체험” is a particular direct experience, mostly a hands-on event.
column5: 그는 오랜 해외 근무 경험이 있다. | 학생들은 농촌에서 일주일 동안 생활을 체험했다.
column6: He has long experience of working overseas. | The students experienced life in the countryside for a week.
column7: Writing “체험이 풍부하다” for rich experience at work. A long record is “경험”; a one-off activity is “체험”.

column4: “비판” is to analyse and judge something critically, giving reasons. “비난” is to blame or condemn someone, often with no intention to improve.
column5: 학자들은 정부의 정책을 비판했다. | 그는 실수 때문에 사람들의 비난을 받았다.
column6: Scholars criticised the government's policy. | He was blamed by people because of the mistake.
column7: Writing “건설적인 비난”. A reasoned critique is “비판”.

column4: “효과” is the result or effect something has. “효율” is efficiency: output compared with input. “효능” is the efficacy of a substance such as a medicine or herb.
column5: 이 약은 두통에 효과가 있다. | 새로운 방식으로 업무 효율을 높였다. | 인삼의 효능이 과학적으로 확인되었다.
column6: This medicine is effective for headaches. | The new method raised work efficiency. | The efficacy of ginseng was confirmed scientifically.
column7: Writing “효율이 있다” for “be effective”. “Effective” is “효과가 있다”; “efficient” is “효율적이다”.

column4: “보전” is to keep something safe and intact so that it is not damaged: “환경 보전”, “재산 보전”. “보존” is to keep something as it is, in its original state: “문화재 보존”, “음식 보존”. “보관” is to keep something in a safe place: “귀중품 보관”.
column5: 우리는 자연환경을 보전해야 한다. | 문화재를 원래의 모습 그대로 보존한다. | 귀중품은 금고에 보관해 주십시오.
column6: We must keep the natural environment safe. | Cultural properties are preserved in their original form. | Please keep valuables in the safe.
column7: Writing “환경 보존” for protecting the environment against damage. “보전” protects, “보존” keeps unchanged.

column4: “너무” means “too much, excessively” and traditionally carries a negative sense. “매우” means “very” and is neutral. In an essay use “매우 / 아주 / 상당히” for a high degree.
column5: 이 가방은 너무 무거워서 들 수 없다. | 이 가방은 매우 가볍다.
column6: This bag is too heavy to lift. | This bag is very light.
column7: Writing “너무 좋다” in a formal essay. The standard meaning of “너무” is excess, so use “매우” instead.

column4: “다시” is “again”, doing something once more from the start or resuming after stopping. “또” is “again, once more” for repetition, and also “and, in addition”.
column5: 시험에 떨어졌지만 다시 도전했다. | 어제도 늦었는데 오늘 또 늦었다.
column6: I failed the exam but took up the challenge again. | I was late yesterday and I was late again today.
column7: Writing “또 시작했다” for “started over after a stop”; “다시” fits better.

column4: “이미” is “already”, stating a completed fact. “벌써” is “already” with a feeling of surprise that something came earlier than expected.
column5: 내가 도착했을 때 회의는 이미 끝나 있었다. | 벌써 열두 시라니 믿기지 않는다.
column6: When I arrived, the meeting had already ended. | I can't believe it is already twelve o'clock.
column7: Using “벌써” in a neutral report. For a plain fact in an essay, “이미” is the safe choice.

column4: “낫다” is to recover or to be better than: “병이 낫다”, “더 낫다”. “낳다” is to give birth or to produce a result. “낮다” is low.
column5: 감기가 다 나았다. | 그녀는 올해 첫째 아이를 낳았다. | 이 지역은 평균 소득이 낮다.
column6: My cold has completely gone. | She gave birth to her first child this year. | Average income in this area is low.
column7: Writing “감기가 낳았다” or “병이 낮다”. Remember: “낳” (with “ㅎ”) is to give birth; “낫” (with “ㅅ”) is to recover.

column4: “부수다” is to smash into pieces: “문을 부수다”. “부시다” is dazzling to the eyes: “눈이 부시다”.
column5: 아이가 장난감을 부수고 말았다. | 눈이 부시게 맑은 하늘이었다.
column6: The child ended up smashing the toy. | The sky was so clear it dazzled the eyes.
column7: Writing “눈이 부수다” or “문을 부시다”.

column4: “썩이다” is used almost only in “속을 썩이다”: to cause someone worry. “썩히다” is to let something rot or go to waste: “재능을 썩히다”.
column5: 아들이 부모의 속을 썩이고 있다. | 좋은 재능을 썩히지 말아야 한다.
column6: The son is causing his parents worry. | You should not let a good talent go to waste.
column7: Writing “속을 썩히다”. With “속” (heart, feelings), it is “썩이다”.

column4: “거치다” is to pass through or go by way of, and to go through a process: “서울을 거쳐”, “심사를 거쳐”. “걸치다” is to extend across a period or area, or to hang something over: “3년에 걸쳐”, “어깨에 걸치다”.
column5: 우리는 서울을 거쳐 부산으로 갔다. | 이 사업은 3년에 걸쳐 진행되었다.
column6: We went to Busan by way of Seoul. | This project was carried out over three years.
column7: Writing “3년을 거쳐” (should be “3년에 걸쳐”) or “심사를 걸쳐” (should be “심사를 거쳐”).

column4: “다리다” is to iron clothes. “달이다” is to boil down herbs or medicine until the essence comes out.
column5: 셔츠를 다려서 입고 나갔다. | 어머니는 약초를 달여 주셨다.
column6: I ironed my shirt, put it on and went out. | My mother brewed herbs for me.
column7: Writing “약을 다리다” or “옷을 달이다”.

column4: “매다” is to tie: “끈을 매다”, “넥타이를 매다”. “메다” is to carry on the shoulder: “가방을 메다”.
column5: 그는 신발 끈을 단단히 맸다. | 그는 어깨에 배낭을 메고 걸었다.
column6: He tied his shoelaces tightly. | He walked with a backpack on his shoulder.
column7: Writing “가방을 매다” or “넥타이를 메다”.

column4: “안치다” is to put food such as rice in a pot to cook. “앉히다” is to make someone sit down.
column5: 쌀을 씻어 솥에 안쳤다. | 엄마는 아이를 의자에 앉혔다.
column6: I washed the rice and put it in the pot. | The mother sat the child on the chair.
column7: Writing “밥을 앉히다”. Cooking rice is “밥을 안치다”.

column4: “조리다” is to simmer meat, fish or vegetables in seasoning until the liquid is almost gone: “생선을 조리다”. “졸이다” is to boil down a liquid, or (“마음을”) to feel anxious: “국물을 졸이다”, “마음을 졸이다”.
column5: 생선을 간장에 조려서 반찬으로 먹었다. | 합격자 발표를 기다리며 마음을 졸였다.
column6: I simmered the fish in soy sauce and ate it as a side dish. | I waited anxiously for the results to be announced.
column7: Writing “마음을 조리다”. Anxiety is always “마음을 졸이다”.

column4: “저리다” is to feel a numb, tingling or aching sensation (“다리가 저리다”). “절이다” is to pickle or salt vegetables or fish.
column5: 오래 앉아 있었더니 다리가 저린다. | 배추를 소금물에 절였다.
column6: My legs are tingling from sitting so long. | I salted the cabbage in brine.
column7: Writing “배추를 저리다”. Pickling is “절이다”.

column4: “벌리다” is to open wide or to create a gap: “입을 벌리다”, “간격을 벌리다”. “벌이다” is to start or carry out something, such as a business, a party or a fight: “사업을 벌이다”, “잔치를 벌이다”.
column5: 아이가 입을 크게 벌렸다. | 그는 새로운 사업을 벌였다.
column6: The child opened his mouth wide. | He started a new business.
column7: Writing “잔치를 벌리다”. For starting an event, a business or a fight it is “벌이다”.

column4: “드러내다” is a transitive verb: to bring something into view on purpose. “드러나다” is intransitive: to become visible by itself.
column5: 그는 자신의 감정을 드러내지 않았다. | 진실이 마침내 드러났다.
column6: He did not show his feelings. | The truth was finally revealed.
column7: Writing “감정이 드러내다” or “진실을 드러났다”. The one who acts takes “을/를 드러내다”; the thing that appears takes “이/가 드러나다”.

column4: “비추다” is transitive: to shine light on something, or to reflect. “비치다” is intransitive: light shines, or something shows through.
column5: 달빛이 조용히 길을 비추었다. | 창문으로 햇빛이 비친다.
column6: The moonlight quietly lit the road. | Sunlight shines through the window.
column7: Writing “햇빛이 방을 비치다”. The sun that lights something “비추다”; the light that comes in “비치다”.

column4: “나타내다” is transitive: to show or express something. “나타나다” is intransitive: to appear or become evident. In a 53 answer both are used for “shows”: the graph “나타내다”, the result “나타나다”.
column5: 이 그래프는 연도별 변화를 나타낸다. | 조사 결과 이러한 경향이 나타났다.
column6: This graph shows the changes by year. | The survey results showed this tendency.
column7: Writing “그래프가 나타났다” or “결과를 나타났다”. Active subject + object → “나타낸다”; result as subject → “나타났다”.

column4: “지나다” is to pass: time or places go past. “지내다” is to spend time or to live in some way.
column5: 벌써 한 달이 지났다. | 요즘 어떻게 지내십니까?
column6: A month has already passed. | How are you doing these days?
column7: Writing “잘 지나세요?” for “how are you?”. Life is “지내다”.

column4: “잊다” is to forget: it is gone from the memory. “잃다” is to lose something: it is gone from your possession.
column5: 약속 시간을 잊고 말았다. | 그는 사고로 지갑을 잃었다.
column6: I forgot the appointed time. | He lost his wallet in an accident.
column7: Writing “지갑을 잊어버렸다” for losing a thing in the street; it is “잃어버렸다”. Only memory is “잊다”.

column4: “안” is a plain negative of choice or fact: not doing. “못” says one cannot do it because of ability or circumstances.
column5: 나는 매운 음식을 안 먹는다. | 나는 매운 음식을 못 먹는다.
column6: I don't eat spicy food. | I can't eat spicy food.
column7: Writing “못 예쁘다”. “못” goes with action verbs; adjectives are negated with “안”.

column4: “작다” is small in size or scale: a room, a voice, a plan. “적다” is few or little in number or amount: people, money, rain. Their opposites are “크다” and “많다”.
column5: 이 방은 크기가 작다. | 시험에 참석한 사람의 수가 적다.
column6: This room is small in size. | The number of people who attended the exam is small.
column7: Writing “사람이 작다” for few people or “크기가 적다” for small size.

column4: “구별” is to tell two things apart by their differences. “구분” is to divide something into categories.
column5: 쌍둥이를 구별하기가 어렵다. | 책을 주제별로 구분하여 정리했다.
column6: It is hard to tell the twins apart. | I sorted the books into groups by subject.
column7: Using the two as one; “구별” is about spotting a difference, “구분” about dividing into groups.

column4: “요구” is a demand, strong and asserting a right. “요청” is a request, polite and asking for help or action.
column5: 노동자들은 임금 인상을 요구했다. | 도움을 요청하는 편지를 보냈다.
column6: The workers demanded a wage increase. | I sent a letter asking for help.
column7: Using “요구” for a polite request. Use “요청” (or “부탁”) when you ask, “요구” when you insist.

column4: “원인” is the cause that produces a result or event. “이유” is the reason that explains an action or an opinion.
column5: 경찰이 사고의 원인을 조사하고 있다. | 그가 떠난 이유를 알 수 없다.
column6: The police are investigating the cause of the accident. | I cannot tell why he left.
column7: Writing “사고의 이유” for the cause of an accident and “결정의 원인” for the reason of a decision.

column4: “해결” is to solve a problem or conflict. “해소” is to dissolve or relieve something unpleasant such as stress, dissatisfaction or tension.
column5: 우리는 문제를 해결할 방법을 찾았다. | 운동은 스트레스를 해소하는 데 도움이 된다.
column6: We found a way to solve the problem. | Exercise helps to relieve stress.
column7: Writing “스트레스를 해결하다”. The condition goes away with “해소”; the problem is closed with “해결”.

column4: “개선” is to make something better, step by step: “환경 개선”. “개정” is to revise an official text such as a law or a book. “개혁” is a fundamental, large-scale reform of a system.
column5: 근로 환경을 개선해야 한다. | 국회는 관련 법률을 개정하였다. | 정부는 교육 제도를 개혁하겠다고 밝혔다.
column6: Working conditions must be improved. | The National Assembly revised the related law. | The government said it would reform the education system.
column7: Using “개정” for any change. “개정” is only for a formal text such as a law; a gradual improvement is “개선” and a whole system is “개혁”.

column4: “강조” is to emphasise a point so that it stands out. “강요” is to force someone to do something.
column5: 선생님은 독서의 중요성을 강조했다. | 부모가 아이에게 공부를 강요해서는 안 된다.
column6: The teacher stressed the importance of reading. | Parents must not force their children to study.
column7: Mixing the two because both have “강”. They share a sound only.

column4: “영향” is influence: a change one thing causes in another, good or bad. “효과” is the intended, usually good effect of an action.
column5: 부모의 태도는 아이에게 큰 영향을 준다. | 운동은 다이어트에 효과가 있다.
column6: Parents' attitudes have a great influence on a child. | Exercise is effective for dieting.
column7: Writing “효과를 받다”. To be influenced is “영향을 받다”; “효과” is something you have (“효과가 있다”).

column4: “-에 대한” points at the target of a feeling or action (“관심”, “태도”, “비판”). “-에 관한” is about a subject or topic (“책”, “연구”, “자료”). “-을/를 위한” is for the benefit or purpose of someone.
column5: 환경 문제에 대한 관심이 높아졌다. | 그는 한국 역사에 관한 책을 읽었다. | 건강을 위한 운동을 시작했다.
column6: Interest in environmental problems has grown. | He read a book about Korean history. | I started exercising for the sake of my health.
column7: Writing “환경에 관한 관심” (target of interest → “대한”) or “아이를 위한 연구” for a study about children (topic → “에 관한”).

column4: All three give a cause. “때문에” is neutral. “덕분에” gives the cause of a good result (thanks to). “탓에” gives the cause of a bad result (because of, blame).
column5: 폭설 때문에 길이 막혔다. | 친구 덕분에 시험에 합격했다. | 내 부주의 탓에 일이 잘못되었다.
column6: The road was blocked because of the heavy snow. | Thanks to my friend, I passed the exam. | The matter went wrong because of my carelessness.
column7: Writing “덕분에” for a bad result (“사고가 나서 덕분에 다쳤다”) or “탓에” for a good one.

column4: “-기 위해(서)” expresses purpose: the aim of an action (to do …). “-기 때문에” expresses cause: why something is so. They cannot be exchanged.
column5: 건강을 지키기 위해 매일 운동한다. | 건강이 나빠졌기 때문에 매일 운동한다.
column6: I exercise every day in order to stay healthy. | I exercise every day because my health has got worse.
column7: Writing “-기 위해” after an adjective or a past tense. Purpose clauses go with verbs and cannot take “-았/었”.

column4: “그러나” (like “하지만”) marks a clear contrast with the previous sentence. “그런데” changes the subject or adds a new twist, with only a mild contrast, and is more common in speech.
column5: 이 방법은 효과가 있다. 그러나 비용이 많이 든다. | 이 방법은 효과가 있다. 그런데 이 방법을 어떻게 적용할 수 있을까?
column6: This method is effective. However, it costs a lot. | This method is effective. By the way, how could it be applied?
column7: Using “그런데” where a clear opposition is meant. In 54 a firm contrast should be “그러나 / 하지만 / 반면에”.

column4: “비교” is to compare things to see similarities and differences. “대조” is to set side by side to check or to stress a difference: “원본과 대조하다”, “대조적이다”. “대비” is “compared to” in numbers (“전년 대비”), or preparing for something (a separate word: “대비하다”).
column5: 두 제품의 가격을 비교해 보았다. | 사본을 원본과 대조해 오류를 찾았다. | 올해 매출은 전년 대비 10% 늘었다.
column6: I compared the prices of the two products. | I checked the copy against the original and found the errors. | This year's sales rose 10% compared with last year.
column7: Writing “전년 비교 10% 증가” in a graph description. The set phrase is “전년 대비 10% 증가”.

column4: “변화” is a change in the nature or state of something. “변동” is a fluctuation, especially in numbers such as prices or rates. “변경” is an alteration someone makes to a plan or a setting.
column5: 사회 구조에 큰 변화가 생겼다. | 환율의 변동이 심해지고 있다. | 회의 일정이 변경되었다.
column6: A great change has occurred in the social structure. | Fluctuations in the exchange rate are growing larger. | The schedule of the meeting has been changed.
column7: Writing “일정이 변화되었다” for a changed appointment; planned changes are “변경”.

column4: “사용” is to use a thing, money or a word. “이용” is to use a facility or service, or to take advantage of someone. “활용” is to make good use of resources, knowledge or skills.
column5: 이 단어는 일상에서 자주 사용된다. | 많은 시민이 대중교통을 이용한다. | 학습한 내용을 실생활에 활용해 보세요.
column6: This word is often used in daily life. | Many citizens use public transport. | Try to put what you have learnt to use in real life.
column7: Writing “대중교통을 사용하다”; services and places are “이용하다”.

column4: “발견” is to find something that already existed but was unknown. “발명” is to invent something that did not exist before.
column5: 그는 새로운 별을 발견했다. | 에디슨은 전구를 발명했다.
column6: He discovered a new star. | Edison invented the light bulb.
column7: Writing “불을 발명했다” for the discovery of fire (it was a discovery). The thing already existed in nature → “발견”.

column4: “제공” is to give or offer something, often information, service or a meal, without asking for a price. “공급” is to supply goods or services in quantity, as in supply and demand.
column5: 학교는 학생들에게 점심을 제공한다. | 전력 공급이 갑자기 중단되었다.
column6: The school provides lunch for the students. | The power supply was suddenly cut off.
column7: Writing “수요와 제공” for supply and demand. The economic term is “수요와 공급”.

column4: “임대” is to lend a property out and receive rent (the owner's side). “임차” is to borrow a property and pay rent (the tenant's side).
column5: 그는 건물을 임대하여 수입을 얻고 있다. | 우리 회사는 사무실을 임차해 사용하고 있다.
column6: He earns income by renting out a building. | Our company rents and uses an office.
column7: Using “임대” for the tenant's side. “임대” = the owner, “임차” = the tenant.

column4: “권리” is a right that a person is entitled to. “권한” is authority that comes with a position or a role.
column5: 모든 국민은 교육을 받을 권리가 있다. | 이 문제는 담당자의 권한 밖의 일이다.
column6: Every citizen has the right to receive education. | This matter is outside the person in charge's authority.
column7: Writing “교육을 받을 권한” for a basic right.

column4: “절약” is to use less so as not to waste: “전기를 절약하다”. “저축” is to put money aside for the future: “은행에 저축하다”.
column5: 에너지를 절약하는 습관이 필요하다. | 그는 매달 월급의 일부를 저축한다.
column6: We need the habit of saving energy. | He saves part of his salary every month.
column7: Writing “전기를 저축하다” for saving electricity.

column4: “소비” is to use up goods, money or energy as a consumer. “소모” is to wear out or use up time, energy or materials.
column5: 가계의 소비가 줄고 있다. | 이 일은 시간과 체력을 많이 소모한다.
column6: Household consumption is falling. | This work wastes a lot of time and strength.
column7: Writing “소모자” for a consumer. The consumer is “소비자”.

column4: “어리다” is for a child or someone not yet grown up (young in age). “젊다” is young as an adult, in the prime of life, not old.
column5: 동생은 아직 어려서 혼자 갈 수 없다. | 그는 나이는 많지만 생각이 젊다.
column6: My younger sibling is still young and cannot go alone. | He is old in years but young in thinking.
column7: Using “어리다” for a twenty-year-old adult. For adults it is “젊다”.

column4: “주의” is attention and caution; it often stands in notices (“주의하십시오”). “조심” is being careful in one's behaviour, with a more everyday tone.
column5: 바닥이 미끄러우니 주의하십시오. | 길이 미끄러우니 조심해서 걸어라.
column6: The floor is slippery, so be careful. | The road is slippery, so walk carefully.
column7: Using “조심하십시오” in a formal notice; “주의하십시오” is the standard sign-board wording.

column4: “익숙하다” is to be familiar with or used to something. “능숙하다” is to be skilled and good at something.
column5: 나는 이곳의 생활에 익숙하다. | 그는 한국어를 능숙하게 말한다.
column6: I am used to life here. | He speaks Korean fluently.
column7: Saying “한국어에 익숙하다” to mean good at Korean. “익숙하다” only says it is not strange to you.

column4: “정확하다” is accurate: with no error. “확실하다” is certain: sure, with no doubt.
column5: 이 계산은 정확하다. | 그가 올 것이라는 것은 확실하다.
column6: This calculation is accurate. | It is certain that he will come.
column7: Using “정확하다” for “sure”. “확실하다” means beyond doubt.

column4: “적절하다” fits the situation or purpose exactly (“적절한 표현”). “적당하다” is suitable or moderate; it can also mean “just enough”, or “half-hearted” (“적당히 하다”).
column5: 이 상황에는 그 표현이 적절하다. | 소금을 적당히 넣어야 맛이 좋다.
column6: That expression is appropriate for this situation. | You must add a suitable amount of salt for it to taste good.
column7: Using “적당히” in a formal essay for “appropriately”; it can sound like “carelessly”. Use “적절히”.

column4: “-(으)로서” marks a status, role or qualification (as a student, as a citizen). “-(으)로써” marks a tool, material, method or a point in time (by means of, with).
column5: 학생으로서 지켜야 할 규칙이 있다. | 대화로써 갈등을 해결할 수 있다.
column6: There are rules to observe as a student. | Conflicts can be solved by means of dialogue.
column7: Writing “학생으로써 책임을 다하다”. If you can say “as a …”, it is “-로서”; if you can say “by using …”, it is “-로써”.

column4: “-든지” (also “-든”) shows a choice, “whichever, whether … or …”. “-던지” is for a past recollection or uncertain reason: “-던지” in “얼마나 … 던지”.
column5: 가든지 말든지 마음대로 해라. | 어제는 얼마나 추웠던지 손이 곱을 정도였다.
column6: Go or don't go, do as you like. | It was so cold yesterday that my hands went numb.
column7: Writing “무엇을 먹던지 좋다” for “whatever you eat is fine”. Choice is “먹든지”; “-던지” recalls the past.

column4: “-(으)러” is used only before “가다 / 오다 / 다니다” and says the purpose of the movement. “-(으)려고” says an intention and works with any verb, and can also be used with a past tense in the main clause.
column5: 친구를 만나러 카페에 갔다. | 시험에 합격하려고 열심히 공부했다.
column6: I went to the café to meet a friend. | I studied hard in order to pass the exam.
column7: Writing “시험에 합격하러 공부했다”. “-러” needs a movement verb after it.

column4: Both turn a verb into a noun. “-(으)ㅁ” names a result or a state and is common in formal writing, notices and titles. “-기” names an action or an activity (“읽기”, “쓰기”) and goes with “위해”, “때문에” and expectations.
column5: 그는 이 방법이 효과적임을 보여 주었다. | 매일 달리기는 건강에 도움이 된다.
column6: He showed that this method is effective. | Running every day is good for health.
column7: Using “-음” for an activity as a subject (“달림은 건강에 좋다”); a named activity is “-기” (“달리기”).

column4: “-(으)ㄴ/는데” (attached) is a connective: background or contrast. “-(으)ㄴ/는 데” (spaced; “데” is a noun meaning “place, point, respect”) is a noun phrase: “in doing …”, “where …”.
column5: 비가 오는데 우산이 없다. | 이 일을 끝내는 데 두 시간이 걸렸다.
column6: It is raining and I have no umbrella. | It took two hours to finish this job.
column7: Dropping the space in “끝내는 데 두 시간이 걸렸다” (here “데” means “in doing”). If “데” could be replaced by “것”, it is the noun and needs the space.

column4: “에게” is the standard written particle for an animate indirect object. “한테” is the spoken form. “께” is the honorific form for someone to be respected.
column5: 선생님은 학생들에게 숙제를 내 주었다. | 어제 친구한테 선물을 받았다. | 할아버지께 편지를 드렸다.
column6: The teacher gave the students homework. | I received a present from a friend yesterday. | I wrote a letter to my grandfather.
column7: Using “한테” in an essay; in 53/54 write “에게”. Never use “에게” or “한테” for the one you respect.

column4: All three give a reason. “-아서/어서” is neutral and cannot be followed by a command or suggestion. “-(으)니까” is a more personal reason and can be followed by a command or suggestion. “-기 때문에” is the formal written reason for essays.
column5: 비가 와서 행사가 취소되었다. | 비가 오니까 우산을 가져가세요. | 비가 오기 때문에 행사가 취소되었다.
column6: The event was cancelled because it rained. | Take an umbrella, since it is raining. | The event was cancelled because of the rain.
column7: Using “-니까” in an essay; essay reasons are “-기 때문에 / -(으)므로”. “-아서” cannot be followed by a request (“비가 와서 우산을 가져가세요” is wrong).
